# **Abstract**
Global university rankings are a worldwide trend that emerged in times of the globalisation and internationalisa‐ tion of higher education. Universities worldwide are now striving to become "world‐class" institutions and are con‐ stantly aiming to improve their ranking position. Global rank‐ ings of universities are thus perceived by many as an ultimate tool for assessing the level of internationalisation at individ‐ ual higher education institutions. This article first discusses the meaning of and relationship between the globalisation and internationalisation of higher education, as their influ‐ ence on the emergence of global rankings is undeniable. It then outlines the methodological designs of four main global university rankings which serve as key prerequisites for the subsequent analyses of both the international(‐isation) indi‐ cators that these rankings include and of the international ranking initiatives that focus exclusively on the international outlook of higher education institutions. In the concluding discussion, the article reveals that, due to the predominantly quantitative orientation of global university rankings (on the internationalisation of higher education), their results should not be generalised or understood as a means to improve the quality of (internationalisation of) higher education.
# **1 **|** INTRODUCTION**
In an era of globalised higher education, global rankings of universities have become a worldwide phenom‐ enon. Although their history is relatively short, they have obtained "a kind of iconic status" (Altbach, 2012, p. 27) among different stakeholders, as they were not designed for a specific stakeholder group but for a
broader audience that is differently involved in higher education (Federkeil, van Vught, & Westerheijden, 2012). Future students see them as an information tool for the selection of their studies, whilst institutional leaders use them as a management and strategic decision‐making instrument (Hazelkorn, 2012; Hazelkorn, Loukkola, & Zhang, 2014). For many governments worldwide, they provide information about the perfor‐ mance of their higher education institutions, whilst profit‐oriented media show an increasing interest because of their ability to create commercial opportunities for the marketing industry (Hazelkorn et al., 2014; Usher & Savino, 2006). Many higher education institutions worldwide are striving to become "world‐class" institutions (Salmi, 2009) to improve their position in the main global rankings. But the impact of these rankings on higher education is not uncontested and neither is their relationship with the internationalisation of higher education (De Wit, 2017). In addition, their methodological designs and indicators are continuously criticised (Federkeil et al., 2012; Hazelkorn, 2012), but many still perceive them as a tool to assess the level of internationalisation at individual higher education institutions.
This article addresses the relationship between the use of metrics by global university rankings and the internationalisation of higher education. It questions the real significance of internationalisation as one of their main categories. As stressed by Altbach (2012, p. 31), "competition, the need to benchmark, and indeed the inevitable logic of globalization make them a permanent part of the 21st‐century academic landscape. The challenge is to understand their nuances, problems, uses – and misuses". To this end, the article first sheds light on the meaning of internationalisation and its relationship with the globalisation of higher education since the emergence of global university rankings was undoubtedly guided by these two contemporary phenomena. It presents the main methodological features of four global rankings as the starting point for the subsequent analysis of the international(‐isation) indicators used by these rankings. In addition, it addresses the emergence of international ranking initiatives that consider internationalisation as their exclusive methodological unit for positioning "international universities" (De Wit, 2015; Knight, 2014). On this basis, the article aims to answer the question of whether the international(‐isation) metrics used by these global rankings represent the inter‐ nationalisation of higher education as a comprehensive process (Delgado‐Márquez, Hurtado‐Torres, & Bondar, 2011). In the concluding discussion, it provides evidence of their mainly quantitative orientation and hence their various limitations. This allows us to understand more precisely the dynamics behind their ability to "measure" the quality of the internationalisation of higher education internationally.
# **2 **|** UNDERSTANDING GLOBALISATION AND INTERNATIONALISATION ** **IN HIGHER EDUCATION**
In ongoing debates on higher education the terms globalisation and internationalisation are often mingled and many authors express contradictory views on their meaning and relationship (Beerkens, 2004; Knight, 2008; Marginson & van der Wende, 2009a; Scott, 1998). Under the auspices of various disciplines, different views on globalisation were suggested as a result of the lack of a generally accepted definition. For "sceptics", globalisa‐ tion is a myth which legitimises "the neoliberal global project, that is, the creation of a global free market and the consolidation of Anglo‐American capitalism within the world's major economic regions" (Held & McGrew, 2003, p. 5). Unlike "sceptics", "globalists" support a multidimensional understanding which considers political, technological, social and cultural factors next to economic ones (Held & McGrew, 2003). According to Beck (2003, p. 37), this multidimension of globalisation is reflected in its "communicational, ecological, organisa‐ tional, cultural, civil and social dimension", but the dominance of globalism reduces it to one single economic dimension and places all other dimensions under the aegis of a world‐market system. Castells (2010) exposes the role of the technological paradigm in his interpretation of globalisation – a new historical reality with its roots in neoliberalism, competitiveness and innovation, promoted by information and communication net‐ works which are key to the functioning of the "network society".
Because of the complex nature of globalisation, its relationship with the internationalisation of higher edu‐ cation is also ambiguous. Both are often used synonymously, despite some notable differences that need to be taken into consideration. For Scott (1998), the existence of independent nation‐states and their relationships are of key importance for the internationalisation of higher education, although individual countries do not re‐ spond in the same way to this trend. But the author notes that globalisation strongly promotes global competi‐ tion between different market blocks, as well as cooperation which results from the global division of labour. In the words of J. Knight (2008, p. 21), the internationalisation of higher education is "the process of integrating an international, intercultural, or global dimension into the purpose, functions or delivery of post‐secondary edu‐ cation", whilst globalisation means ''the flow of people, culture, ideas, values, knowledge, technology and econ‐ omy across borders resulting in a more interconnected and interdependent world" (p. 4). Here, globalisation affects internationalisation, which "is changing the world of higher education" (Knight, 2008, p. 1). According to Marginson and van der Wende (2009a, pp. 21–23), internationalisation occurs between people or individual higher education institutions within different national systems and refers to relationships that extend beyond the borders of nation‐states, whilst globalisation occurs in many countries and connects the global, national and local dimensions of higher education. All authors stress that the relationship between globalisation and internationalisation is dialectical, since globalisation is not "a higher form of internationalisation" (Scott, 1998, p. 124), whilst internationalisation is "both a reaction to and a driver for globalisation" (Beerkens, 2004, p. 24). As such, the internationalisation of higher education is not solely a response to globalisation, as it is often ar‐ gued (Knight, 2008), because "[a]s long as we do not live in a truly globalised world […], globalisation will shape international flows and these flows [will] again foster globalisation" (Beerkens, 2004, p. 17).
# **3 **|** THE RISING INFLUENCE OF GLOBAL UNIVERSIT Y R ANKINGS ON ** **HIGHER EDUCATION**
The globalisation and internationalisation of higher education undeniably contributed to the emergence of the world's main university rankings, understood here as an "international comparison of institutional per‐ formance and reputation" (Hazelkorn, 2011, cited in Hazelkorn, 2012, p. 342). The first initiative, known as the Academic Ranking of World Universities (ARWU) or Shanghai ranking, was published in 2003 by the Centre for World‐Class Universities of Jiao Tong University. Its launch encouraged many imitators and vis‐ ibly affected the development of this field. A year later (2004), the Times Higher Education World University Ranking (hereafter the THE ranking) was published on the basis of THE's cooperation with Quacquarelli‐ Symonds (QS) which lasted until 2009 (known as the THE‐QS ranking). In 2010, THE began working with Thomas Reuters and fundamentally changed its methodology, whilst QS set up its own university rank‐ ing system, known as the QS World University Ranking (hereafter the QS ranking). For slightly over half (52%) of the participants in the survey of the European University Association (EUA) on rankings and institu‐ tional strategies, the QS ranking is the most influential, followed by the THE ranking (50%) and ARWU (48%) (Hazelkorn et al., 2014). But in response to methodological criticisms of these initial initiatives, some supra‐ national organisations began to promote the establishment of alternative ranking systems. The EU sponsored the launch of the European multidimensional ranking, commonly known as U‐Multirank, which was designed to ensure a greater transparency of European higher education by offering detailed information on specific institutional profiles and performance (Hazelkorn, 2012; Westerheijden, 2015). For this discussion, it is es‐ sential to examine the main methodological characteristics of the four selected global rankings (i.e., ARWU, the THE and QS rankings, U‐Multirank) in terms of their key categories and indicators, since it is only on this basis that one can continue with the analysis of their international(‐isation) metrics.

## **3.1 **|** Internationalisation of higher education and global university rankings**
ARWU refers only indirectly to the international element of universities. As outlined by Delgado‐Márquez et al. (2011, p. 273), it "does not emphasize any indicator which could directly fit for the measurement of internation‐ alization of an HEI […] [but] considers internationalization in an indirect way, since an institution's performance and size depend on some internationalization components". These components are included in the category on institutional per capita performance which considers full‐time equivalent academic staff, but does not distinguish between foreign and domestic academic staff. However, the total weight attached to this category represents only one tenth of the final ranking score and, compared to some other categories used by ARWU (e.g., Quality of faculty or Research output – each 40% of the final ranking score), it is of rather marginal importance (ARWU, 2017; Delgado‐Márquez et al., 2011).
Unlike ARWU, the THE ranking includes the international outlook of universities among its five main catego‐ ries. Its weight is much weaker (7.5% in total) than most of the other four, although with the latest methodological updates its total weighted score was more evenly distributed among performance indicators on international students and staff (i.e., international‐to‐domestic‐student and staff ratio) and international cooperation (2.5% each) (THE, 2017). The QS ranking also refers to the ratio of international students and faculty as two of its main categories which jointly represent 10% of the final ranking score. Performance indicators representing these two categories are the proportion of students and faculty who are international (5% each), but again, their value is rather limited compared to some other categories for ranking universities (QS, 2017).
As regards U‐Multirank, 14 indicators constitute the category on the international orientation of higher educa‐ tion institutions and refer to institutional internationalisation activities (e.g., study abroad, student mobility), inter‐ national academic staff, international orientation of undergraduate and master programmes or doctorate degrees, joint publications, research grants, etc. Unlike the predominant focus of both the THE and QS rankings on the proportion of international students and academic staff (or co‐authored publications in the case of the THE rank‐ ing), it uses indicators that are related to incoming and outgoing, temporary and degree mobile students, as well as the international orientation of study programmes, the use of foreign (English) language, etc. (U‐Multirank, 2018). As stressed by Westerheijden (2015, p. 431), U‐Multirank's methodological soundness is in its validity because its indicators "inform as directly as possible about a university's performances (outputs) rather than concentrating on more readily available information on inputs and conditions (income, staff numbers, etc.)".
Nevertheless, the discussion above shows that, compared to other ranking categories such as Research, Teaching, or Citations, the category and corresponding indicators on the internationalisation of higher education represent only a maximum of one tenth of the overall assessment score (7.5% in the case of the THE ranking and 10% in the case of the QS ranking). Exceptions are U‐Multirank, which does not "measure" quantitatively the weight attached to individual indicators, and ARWU in which internationalisation per se does not play a role, mainly because of its focus on institutional research performance.
## **3.2 **|** Ranking and rating universities on the internationalisation of higher education**
We have recently witnessed the launch of different international ranking initiatives that focus exclusively on the international element of universities. In 2014, the THE journal started to publish a list of the world's 100 most in‐ ternational universities by drawing on data from the THE ranking and its performance indicators on international‐ to domestic‐student and staff ratio and international collaboration in the category International outlook. In 2017, THE began to use data from the Academic Reputation Survey in order to rank the 150 world's most international universities, whilst in 2018, the number of universities included in this ranking rose to 200 (THE, 2018). The three highest‐ranked universities are found in relatively small countries, such as Switzerland, Hong Kong and Singapore. From the beginning, two Swiss universities (ETH Zürich – Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Zürich and the École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne) have occupied the leading two positions. Both have the highest av‐ erage proportion of international staff and international co‐authored publications (62% each) (Bothwell, 2017), reflecting the fact that the size of individual higher education systems does not reduce the influx of international students and academic staff.
QS also developed a university rating system for internationalisation known as QS Stars. It differs from the ranking system: whilst ranking compares institutions and asks "who is the best?", rating asks "who is good on what?" and judges institutional performance against a set of standards by giving a score to each category and to the overall assessment (QS Intelligent Unit, n.d.). To measure progress towards internationalisation, QS stars uses seven criteria: Institutional research collaborations (50 points), International faculty and students (20 points each), International student support – religious facilities (10 points), Inbound and outbound exchange students (20 points each) and International diversity (10 points). For each criterion, maximum points are awarded if the institution meets the following conditions: collaboration with 50 or more universities ranked in QS; 25% or more international students or 20% or more international staff; one or more places for practising three or more major religions; 2% or more of incoming or outgoing students in the total student population and at least 50 nationali‐ ties in the overall student population (QS, 2014). In 2018, the three leading positions were occupied by Aalborg University in Denmark (5 stars), Aim Shams University in Egypt (4 stars) and Al‐Farabi Kazakh National University in Kazakhstan (5 stars), whilst among the "top" ten institutions, four universities from English‐speaking countries were also included – three are based in the UK and one in Australia (QS, 2018).
However, "it is not possible to produce a definitive list of the worlds' 'top performing' universities in terms of international orientation because a comprehensive database of institutional performance in the different areas of internationalisation is not available" (U‐Multirank, 2015, p. 1). To overcome this limitation, U‐Multirank published in 2015 a ready‐made ranking of the international orientation of universities which included indicators on student mobility, international academic staff, international joint publications and international doctorate degrees. Unlike the THE's ranking of the world's most international universities or the QS Stars rating system on internationalisa‐ tion, which both collect information on the share of international students and academic staff (or on international collaboration in the case of the THE's ranking), U‐Multirank also refers to other aspects of internationalisation and considers different types of higher education institutions (e.g., business schools, specialised universities, techni‐ cally‐oriented institutions, etc. (U‐Multirank, 2015). In 2015, out of 237 PhD awarding institutions with more than 7.5% international students, 27 obtained top marks in all four indicators. All are located in Europe: 6 in France, 4 in Austria, 3 in Belgium and the Netherlands (U‐Multirank, 2015).
The debate above also uses a new popular term "international university" whose characteristics were ad‐ dressed by several authors. J. Knight (2014, p. 139–140) identified three generations of international universities. The first, which most commonly uses this fashionable phrase, supports multiple international activities, such as student and staff mobility or joint programmes with partners from abroad. Universities from the second gener‐ ation usually establish branch campuses or satellite offices abroad, whilst the third generation is often jointly funded and developed by foreign partner institutions. However, very few meet all the criteria for being an "inter‐ national university" (De Wit, 2015) and in certain parts of the world, e.g., in developing countries, many of their

In addition, De Wit (2015, p. 7) draws attention to the following: "more and more universities in the future will refer, in their mission statements and policies, […] that they are an international university, without clearly explaining what they mean by it". In their internationalisation policies and strategies, they (still) predominantly focus on the internationalisation dimension "abroad" in which the recruitment of talented international students and scholars, the establishment of branch campuses abroad, the development of joint and double degree programmes, etc. are supported (Knight, 2014). Nevertheless, De Wit (2017, p. 27) notes that this focus on internationalisation "abroad" suggests that (too) many higher education institutions still perceive internationalisation as a group of unrelated and fragmented activities, although it also means "preparing graduates to be internationally knowledgeable and interculturally skilled, able to live and work in more culturally diverse communities both at home and abroad" (Knight, 2008, p. 14).
# **4 **|** DISCUSSION**
The analysis of the international(‐isation) element in global rankings of universities shows that most of the global rankings consider only a few easily quantifiable indicators on the proportion of international students and aca‐ demic staff or co‐authored publications (De Wit, 2015, 2017; Delgado‐Márquez et al., 2011). But only few univer‐ sities score highly in these two or three commonly‐used indicators, unlike the great majority of higher education institutions which do not occupy such highly‐ranked positions. Even though these international(‐isation) metrics only account for a maximum of 10% of the final ranking score, global university rankings are still perceived by many as key drivers for internationalisation, with a strong impact on national and institutional policies and strate‐ gies for internationalisation, as emphasised by De Wit (2017, p. 26).
At the national level, many governments in developed (mainly Western) countries adopted "excellence initia‐ tives". According to Bleiklie (2011, p. 21), this concept is at the centre of transformations of higher education and "refers to an outstanding high level of quality that distinguishes the best universities from the rest". One excel‐ lence‐based initiative was launched in Germany where a group of research‐intensive universities was selected to improve their position in the world's main university rankings. In addition to these selective mechanisms for allocating financial resources, some governments also consider the position of their universities in rankings in decision‐making processes to grant accreditation (Bleiklie, 2011; Hazelkorn, 2012). Therefore, it should be taken into consideration that:
global university rankings take global relativisation further and centre it at the institutional level. In each nation governments, media and public are fascinated by the comparative global perfor‐ mance of "their" institutions, which becomes treated as a matter of significant national interest. (Marginson & van der Wende, 2009a, p. 25)
Hence, it is not surprising that the success of higher education institutions increasingly depends on their ability to improve their position in the main global university rankings which influence institutional policy discourses. The University of Ljubljana, which is the only Slovene university ranked among 500 in ARWU, stated in its long‐term university strategy (2012–2020) that "[i]ts ambition is to be ranked among the 250 best universities in the world on
various rankings, […] especially with more internationalization" (University of Ljubljana, 2012). Hence, it is not un‐ common for higher education institutions to define their main activities according to the principal indicators of these rankings (De Wit, 2017). As was seen in the aforementioned EUA survey, the main indicator to which institutions pay attention in strategic planning or internal monitoring of activities is the number of international students (Hazelkorn et al., 2014). This coincides with the fact that global university rankings appeared in times of greater student mobility and with "the idea that mobility in the 21st century is no longer just national […] but global" (Westerheijden, 2015, p. 420). In addition, this suggests that internationalisation should no longer refer only to relationships between national systems of higher education, but also between the global and local dimension of higher education, although in the years to come, major misconceptions on the internationalisation of higher education will probably be that it is "being equal to 'global' and ignoring 'local' […] [or that is] being a risk for national and cultural identities" (De Wit, 2017, p. 28).
According to OECD (2017), the number of students enrolled in tertiary education abroad rose from 0.8 million in the 1970s to 4.6 million at present. But student mobility flows also manifest global imbalances, since coun‐ tries and institutions that widely use English as their *lingua franca* attract the highest proportion of international students and academic staff and often occupy the highest positions in global university rankings. In this respect, Marginson and van der Wende (2009a, p.32) called attention to the following:
Many students from non‐English‐speaking nations want to acquire English and degrees from English‐speaking systems, while comparatively few English‐speaking students want to acquire other languages and degrees from non‐English‐speaking nations. The driver here is the vertical patterning of language and degree status. […] The global academic role of English is as much driven by the weight of the Anglo‐American bloc within the world economy, the cultural industries and the Internet, as by specific developments in higher education.
Imbalances in global mobility flows can thus also be viewed as a result of distinct economic, political, technological and cultural factors that are seen by the "globalists" as an outcome of the multidimensional character of globalisation (Held & McGrew, 2003), the latter being of key importance for the functioning of the "network society" to paraphrase Castells (Castells, 2010). But Beck (2003) argues that it was globalism that reduced these multidimensional factors to one sole economic dimension, whilst De Wit, Gacel‐Ávila, Jones, and Jooste (2017) underlined that, due to increas‐ ingly influential economic rationales, we have already entered the phase of the *globalisation of internationalisation* in which the development of commercially‐oriented forms of cross‐border activities is (strongly) supported.
Another issue concerning global rankings' attention to the international(‐isation) element of universities is the importance attached to international co‐authored publications. Authors who publish in languages other than English are at a disadvantage in relation to those from English‐speaking countries who publish more easily in rec‐ ognised international journals. In addition, the English bibliometric databases used by global rankings must also be questioned (Federkeil et al., 2012; Hazelkorn, 2012; Hazelkorn et al., 2014; Westerheijden, 2015). As stressed by Altbach (2012, p. 29), the advantage of academic institutions from the world's major (Western) knowledge centres caused the formation of centres and peripheries which result from their "significant head starts provided by their histories, wealth, ability to attract top scholars and students worldwide, strong traditions of academic freedom, and academic cultures based on competition and meritocracy".
# **5 **|** CONCLUSIONS**
The link between the internationalisation and globalisation of higher education proved to be undeniable and, like the internationalisation of higher education, global rankings of universities are also perceived as "another cause and effect of the globalisation of higher education" (Marginson & van der Wende, 2009b, p. 122). Despite the fact that the inclusion of categories and performance indicators representing the internationalisation of higher
education is still quite a novelty for such transparency instruments (Hazelkorn, 2012), they are a prime example of rankings' direct impact on the internationalisation of higher education, whilst their indirect impact is characterised by internationalisation policies and strategies at the national and institutional level of higher education (De Wit, 2017, p. 26). Since both national and institutional policies and strategies for internationalisation centre on rank‐ ings' main requirements (e.g., increasing the proportion of international students or academic staff), they support the misleading idea that internationalisation means recruiting many (talented) international students or scholars or that it is similar to teaching in English (De Wit, 2017). But it is a more comprehensive process, consisting also of the "at home" dimension which is interdependently related to the "abroad" component (Knight, 2008) through the development of international, intercultural and global learning outcomes or responsible global citizenship, col‐ laboration in joint research projects, etc. (De Wit, 2017, p. 27).
The prevalence given to the recruitment of many talented students or scholars from abroad is also associated with the global rankings' focus on research performance as the main criterion for institutional excellence. Other core missions, such as teaching or the third mission are still largely overlooked by most global university rankings, in particular ARWU (Westerheijden, 2015). Some, such as the THE ranking, did design various proxies to measure the quality of teaching, but, according to Altbach (2012, p. 28), "[t]he problem is that these proxies do not actually measure teaching quality or come close to assessing its impact on learning". On the other hand, U‐Multirank's Teaching & Learning category also contains indicators such as Innovative forms of teaching and assessment or Community service learning, and in this respect it (also) differs from other global ranking initiatives (U‐Multirank, 2018).
By prioritising the research function of higher education institutions, global rankings also privilege "world‐ class" universities whose key characteristics are a high concentration of talent, abundant resources for conducting advanced research and favourable governance (Salmi, 2009). But only few universities are world's "top" institu‐ tions and they are only found in a limited number of mostly Western countries, although there are over 18,500 institutions located in 186 countries worldwide, according to the World Higher Education Database (International Association of Universities, 2018). As such, global rankings disadvantage those institutions in which research is not their primary mission. Bleiklie thus perceives them as one of the "three major mechanisms that contribute to shaping the hierarchies that constitute the vertical diversity of a higher education system", next to accreditation and funding (Bleiklie, 2011, p. 24). Not only do they overlook differences between research‐intensive univer‐ sities or between research universities and other types of institutions, they also obscure differences between and within individual departments or disciplinary fields (Federkeil et al., 2012; Hazelkorn, 2012; Hazelkorn et al., 2014; Marginson & van der Wende, 2009a; Westerheijden, 2015). Here, it should be added that the proportion of international students varies greatly between academic disciplines and, as is well‐known, most students choose to enrol in English‐taught programmes in the fields of business, economics, management, international law, engi‐ neering, etc.
Hence, the results of global university rankings (e.g., on the internationalisation of higher education) "should not be overly generalised" (Hazelkorn et al., 2014, p. 45). They propose a "one size fits all" approach to "measure" the quality of higher education internationally and prioritise quantity over quality (Usher & Savino, 2006, p. 34). But as underlined by Cameron (1963, p. 13), "not everything that can be counted counts, and not everything that counts can be counted" because global rankings can only suggest "that some institutions or disciplines are more important [but] not necessarily better than others" (Hazelkorn, 2012, p. 354), as there is no evidence that the quality of the internationalisation of an individual institution would be improved by moving up the ranking ladder. It can thus be concluded that global university rankings easily "become an end in themselves without regard to exactly what they measure or whether they contribute to institutional and system improvement" (Marginson & van der Wende, 2009b, p. 126). If also the internationalisation of higher education is perceived as a goal in itself, then it cannot serve as a means for improving the quality of higher education, research and service to society (De Wit, 2015).
